title: Validation and error handling
intro: A backend must never trust data just because the React frontend already validated it. In this lesson, you will add Bean Validation to Spring Boot DTOs, turn validation and business errors into consistent HTTP responses, and give the React application useful field-level error information.
body:
## Why validate on the backend?

Imagine that your React task form refuses to submit an empty title. That is useful for the user, but it is not a security boundary.

A client can send HTTP requests without using your React application at all. A user can use curl, Postman, a script, or another application to call the API directly.

That means the backend must validate every request it accepts.

**Frontend validation improves the user experience; backend validation protects the integrity of your application.**

For example, your React application might check that a task title is not empty. Spring Boot must perform the same check before accepting the request.

Our task manager will eventually receive requests such as:

~~~json
{
  "title": "Learn Spring Boot",
  "dueDate": "2026-10-15",
  "priority": "high"
}
~~~

The backend needs to decide whether this data is valid before it reaches business logic or the database.

## Bean Validation

Spring Boot supports **Bean Validation**, a standard Java validation API implemented by libraries such as Hibernate Validator.

Bean Validation lets you describe constraints directly on DTO fields or record components using annotations.

For example:

~~~java
public record CreateTaskRequest(
    @NotBlank
    @Size(max = 100)
    String title
) {}
~~~

`@NotBlank` means the value must not be null, empty, or consist only of whitespace.

`@Size(max = 100)` limits the length to 100 characters.

The advantage is that the validation rules are visible next to the DTO definition rather than being scattered through controller code.

Spring Boot's validation documentation is available in the [Spring Boot reference documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/io/validation.html).

## Common validation annotations

Several Bean Validation annotations are especially useful for REST APIs.

`@NotBlank` is useful for required text:

~~~java
@NotBlank
String title
~~~

`@Size` can restrict the size of strings or collections:

~~~java
@Size(max = 100)
String title
~~~

`@Email` checks that a string has an email-like format:

~~~java
@Email
String email
~~~

`@Min` requires a numeric value to be at least the specified minimum:

~~~java
@Min(1)
int quantity
~~~

`@Future` requires a date or date-time value to represent a future point in time:

~~~java
@Future
LocalDate dueDate
~~~

For optional fields, remember that many constraints such as `@Future` generally allow `null`. If the field must also be present, combine an appropriate presence constraint with the value constraint.

For example:

~~~java
@NotNull
@Future
LocalDate dueDate
~~~

means that a due date is required and must be in the future.

## Validate the request body

Adding annotations to a DTO does not automatically mean every controller argument is validated. Tell Spring to validate the request body with `@Valid`.

~~~java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> create(
    @Valid @RequestBody CreateTaskRequest request
) {
    TaskResponse task = taskService.create(request);

    return ResponseEntity
        .created(URI.create("/api/tasks/" + task.id()))
        .body(task);
}
~~~

`@RequestBody` tells Spring to deserialize JSON into the DTO.

`@Valid` tells Spring to run Bean Validation against that DTO before the controller method continues.

This gives you an important boundary:

~~~text
HTTP JSON
   ↓
Jackson
   ↓
CreateTaskRequest
   ↓
Bean Validation
   ↓
Controller method
   ↓
Business logic
~~~

If validation fails, the controller method does not continue normally.

## What happens when validation fails?

Suppose the client sends:

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "From bad input to a clear answer", "nodes": [{"id": "c", "label": "POST { \"title\": \"\" }", "kind": "client"}, {"id": "v", "label": "@Valid", "sub": "@NotBlank fails", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "ex", "label": "MethodArgumentNotValidException", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "adv", "label": "@RestControllerAdvice", "sub": "one handler for all", "highlight": true}, {"id": "r", "label": "400 Problem Details", "sub": "{ errors: { title: … } }", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "c", "to": "v"}, {"from": "v", "to": "ex", "label": "throws"}, {"from": "ex", "to": "adv"}, {"from": "adv", "to": "r"}]}
~~~

~~~json
{
  "title": ""
}
~~~

The `@NotBlank` constraint fails.

For a `@Valid @RequestBody` argument, Spring raises a `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. This exception represents a validation failure while binding and validating the request body.

Spring normally treats this as a client error and the HTTP response should be `400 Bad Request`.

The important part is that your API should return a useful, consistent error structure instead of exposing an internal Java exception or stack trace.

## Business rules are different

Not every error is a simple DTO validation error.

~~~terms
[{"term": "Validation", "def": "Is the input well-formed? Blank title, bad email, negative quantity → **400**."}, {"term": "Business rule", "def": "Is the action allowed right now? Duplicate title, sold-out product, closed ticket → **409** or **422**."}]
~~~

Consider a request for:

~~~text
GET /api/tasks/999
~~~

The request can be perfectly valid syntactically. The problem is that task 999 does not exist.

This is a business/application-level condition, so we can represent it with a custom exception:

~~~java
public class TaskNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    public TaskNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super("Task not found: " + id);
    }
}
~~~

The service can throw it when the requested task cannot be found.

~~~java
Task task = repository.findById(id)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new TaskNotFoundException(id));
~~~

The controller does not need to contain a `try/catch` around every service call. We can handle these exceptions centrally.

## @RestControllerAdvice

Spring provides `@RestControllerAdvice` for global REST exception handling.

It allows you to define how exceptions from controllers should become HTTP responses.

For example:

~~~java
@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(TaskNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleTaskNotFound(
        TaskNotFoundException exception
    ) {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail
            .forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, exception.getMessage());

        problem.setTitle("Task Not Found");

        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(problem);
    }
}
~~~

`@ExceptionHandler` connects a Java exception type to a handler method.

This creates a clean separation: the service reports what went wrong, while the web layer decides how that error is represented over HTTP.

## Problem Details

For REST APIs, Spring supports **Problem Details for HTTP APIs**, based on RFC 9457.

Spring's `ProblemDetail` gives us a standard structure for describing HTTP errors. It includes fields such as `type`, `title`, `status` and `detail`.

For a validation error, we can additionally include an `errors` property containing field-level information.

For example:

~~~json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Validation failed",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "must not be blank"
    }
  ]
}
~~~

The `errors` property is an extension to the standard Problem Details properties. It is particularly useful for form-based applications because the frontend can associate each message with a specific field.

Spring's `ProblemDetail` API is documented in the [Spring Framework web documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-ann-rest-exceptions.html).

## Handling validation errors centrally

A validation exception handler can inspect the validation errors and convert them into a simple API structure.

A simplified version might look like this:

~~~java
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleValidation(
    MethodArgumentNotValidException exception
) {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
        HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
        "Validation failed"
    );

    problem.setTitle("Bad Request");

    List<Map<String, String>> errors = exception.getBindingResult()
        .getFieldErrors()
        .stream()
        .map(error -> Map.of(
            "field", error.getField(),
            "message", error.getDefaultMessage()
        ))
        .toList();

    problem.setProperty("errors", errors);

    return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem);
}
~~~

The exact handler can become more sophisticated later, but the important idea is straightforward: transform Spring's internal validation information into a stable API contract.

## Other HTTP errors

A useful API establishes predictable meanings for common failures.

A malformed or invalid request can result in `400 Bad Request`.

A requested task that does not exist can result in `404 Not Found`.

A request that conflicts with an existing resource or application state can result in `409 Conflict`.

For example, imagine that task titles eventually need to be unique. Creating another task with an existing title could produce:

~~~json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "A task with this title already exists"
}
~~~

The exact business rules depend on the application, but the principle stays the same: **use HTTP status codes to communicate the category of the problem and the response body to explain it.**

## Never leak stack traces

A stack trace is useful to the developer running the backend, but it is not an appropriate API response for a normal client error.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Leaky error", "lang": "json", "code": "{\n  \"error\": \"org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: duplicate key value violates unique constraint \\\"task_title_key\\\"\",\n  \"trace\": \"at com.zaxxer.hikari…\"\n}", "note": "Exposes your stack, tables and libraries."}, "right": {"title": "Problem Details", "lang": "json", "code": "{\n  \"type\": \"about:blank\",\n  \"title\": \"Conflict\",\n  \"status\": 409,\n  \"detail\": \"A task with this title already exists.\"\n}", "note": "Helpful for the client, safe for you. Log the details server-side."}}
~~~

Do not return responses containing details such as:

~~~text
java.lang.NullPointerException
at hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager...
...
~~~

Such information can reveal internal class names, database details, file paths or implementation decisions.

Instead, return a controlled Problem Details response to the client and log the technical details on the server.

For an unexpected server error, the client might receive a generic `500 Internal Server Error` response while the backend log contains the full exception and stack trace.

## Logging errors

Logging means recording useful information about application behaviour so developers and operators can investigate problems.

Spring applications commonly use a logging facade such as SLF4J through Spring Boot's logging setup.

For example:

~~~java
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApiExceptionHandler.class);
~~~

Then:

~~~java
log.error("Unexpected error while processing request", exception);
~~~

Do not log passwords, authentication tokens, payment details or other sensitive information merely because an exception occurred.

A good rule is: **give the client the information it needs to understand the API error, and give the server logs the information developers need to diagnose the problem.**

## How React uses the error response

The consistent error format makes the frontend much easier to build.

Suppose React sends:

~~~json
{
  "title": ""
}
~~~

and receives:

~~~json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Validation failed",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "must not be blank"
    }
  ]
}
~~~

The React application can parse the `errors` array and put the message next to the corresponding form control.

Conceptually:

~~~text
API response
    ↓
errors[]
    ↓
field = "title"
    ↓
set title field error
    ↓
"must not be blank"
~~~

This is much more useful than displaying a generic message such as `Something went wrong` for every failure.

## Validation belongs at multiple boundaries

You may notice that some validation rules appear in several places.

The React form validates data because users need immediate feedback.

The REST API validates data because clients cannot be trusted.

The database can enforce certain constraints because data integrity should survive even if another application writes to the database.

These layers have different responsibilities. Duplicating a simple rule across boundaries is not necessarily bad when each layer needs to protect itself.

For example, a database uniqueness constraint can protect data integrity even if an API bug accidentally allows two requests through at almost the same time.

## Common mistakes

### Trusting frontend validation

React validation is helpful, but a client can bypass it completely. Always validate data at the backend boundary.

### Forgetting @Valid

Adding `@NotBlank` to a DTO does not help if the request body is never validated. Use `@Valid @RequestBody` for request DTOs that should be validated.

### Returning different error shapes

If one endpoint returns `{ "error": "..." }` and another returns a completely different structure, frontend error handling becomes unnecessarily complicated. Establish a consistent Problem Details format.

### Returning stack traces to clients

Keep diagnostic details in server-side logs. Return a controlled response to the client.

### Treating every error as 500

A missing task is not necessarily a server failure. Use `404` for a missing resource and `400` for invalid input. Reserve `500` for unexpected server-side failures.

### Mixing validation and business logic

`@Size(max = 100)` is a straightforward input constraint. Whether a task can be completed after a particular business event is a different kind of rule and belongs in application logic.

## The complete error flow

Your task manager now has a useful error-handling architecture:

~~~text
React request
    ↓
@RequestBody DTO
    ↓
@Valid
    ↓
Bean Validation
    ↓
400 ProblemDetail

Valid request
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
TaskNotFoundException
    ↓
@RestControllerAdvice
    ↓
404 ProblemDetail
~~~

This structure means the controller does not need to understand every possible failure. It delegates application work to the service and lets the global exception handler translate known failures into a consistent HTTP API.

In the next lesson, we will put these responsibilities into a layered architecture. You will separate controllers, services and repositories so that the task manager can grow without turning one controller into the entire application.
takeaways: Backend validation is required even when the React application already validates the same form.
Bean Validation annotations such as @NotBlank, @Size, @Email, @Min and @Future describe common DTO constraints.
A @RestControllerAdvice can translate validation and business exceptions into consistent HTTP responses.
ProblemDetail provides a standard error structure, which can be extended with an errors array for field-level validation messages.
Clients should receive safe error information while detailed exception information stays in server-side logs.

quiz.question: Why must the Spring Boot backend validate a task title even if React already validates it?
options: React validation is automatically disabled after deployment
HTTP clients can bypass React and call the API directly
Spring Boot cannot receive data from React
Bean Validation only works when React sends invalid data
quiz.explanation: Any client can call the HTTP API directly, so the backend must enforce its own input rules.

quiz.question: What does @Valid do when used with @RequestBody?
options: It converts Java into JSON
It starts the embedded Tomcat server
It tells Spring to validate the deserialized request object
It automatically saves the DTO to PostgreSQL
quiz.explanation: @Valid triggers Bean Validation after Spring has converted the request body into the DTO.

quiz.question: What happens when a @NotBlank constraint fails on a @Valid request body?
options: Spring can raise MethodArgumentNotValidException and return a 400 response
Spring automatically returns 201 Created
The application must always shut down
Spring silently ignores the invalid field
quiz.explanation: A validation failure during request-body binding results in MethodArgumentNotValidException, which can be handled as a 400 Bad Request.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of @RestControllerAdvice?
options: To define database tables
To create React components
To replace Maven
To handle controller exceptions centrally and turn them into HTTP responses
quiz.explanation: @RestControllerAdvice provides centralized exception handling for REST controllers.

options: Restart the Spring Boot server
Associate a validation message with a specific form field
Change the database schema automatically
Determine which HTTP method created the request
quiz.explanation: The field property tells the frontend where to display the corresponding validation message.

exercise.title: Build a validation and Problem Details response
exercise.task: Write validateTask(dto) to mirror the validation rules of a Spring Boot task DTO. Return an array of objects shaped as { field, message }, and return an empty array when the DTO is valid. The title is required and must not be blank; when invalid for this rule, return { field: "title", message: "must not be blank" }. The title must also be at most 100 characters; when it is too long, return { field: "title", message: "size must be at most 100" }. If dueDate is provided, it must be a valid ISO date string in exactly YYYY-MM-DD form; otherwise return { field: "dueDate", message: "must be a valid date" }. If priority is provided, it must be exactly one of "low", "normal", or "high"; otherwise return { field: "priority", message: "must be one of low, normal, high" }. Return every applicable error rather than stopping after the first one. Also implement toProblemDetail(errors), returning exactly { type: "about:blank", title: "Bad Request", status: 400, detail: "Validation failed", errors }. This mirrors the shape a Spring @RestControllerAdvice can return using ProblemDetail. The real Java implementation uses Bean Validation and Spring's exception handling; this browser exercise mirrors the design in TypeScript.
exercise.hint: Check the title for undefined or whitespace-only content before checking its length. For the date, validate both the exact YYYY-MM-DD format and whether the calendar date actually exists; for example, 2026-02-31 must be rejected. For priority, use an explicit list of the three allowed values. Add every applicable error to the array instead of returning early.

tests.name: It rejects a missing title
tests.code:
const errors = validateTask({});
return errors.length === 1 && errors[0].field === "title" && errors[0].message === "must not be blank";

tests.name: It rejects an overly long title
It rejects an invalid calendar date
tests.code:
const errors = validateTask({ title: "Task", dueDate: "2026-02-31" });
return errors.length === 1 && errors[0].field === "dueDate" && errors[0].message === "must be a valid date";

tests.name: It rejects an invalid priority
tests.code:
const errors = validateTask({ title: "Task", priority: "urgent" });
return errors.length === 1 && errors[0].field === "priority" && errors[0].message === "must be one of low, normal, high";

tests.name: It returns valid data and the Problem Details shape
